docs.text: swjtumover ¶ ROS 2 software for the swjtumover robot. It provides the motor driver, the display driver, a LiDAR adapter, line following, navigation and the line-then-home mission. There are two ways to operate it, and both are first-class: Running on the robot — direct ros2 launch and ros2 run commands. Running with caasi — deploy, build, run and monitor from another machine. For a side-by-side list of every command, see Commands and workflows . Before driving the robot, read Hardware and safety . For multi-robot naming and seeing the robot's screen remotely, see Remote access . What is in the package ¶ package contents swjtumover_msgs MotorState : header, phase current, rpm, position, five fault flags swjtumover_bringup motor driver, screen driver, launch files, configuration, task scripts swjtumover_vanjee LiDAR adapter publishing /scan The robot ¶ item value body 0.32 × 0.30 m, 0.089 m tall LiDAR Vanjee 718H, single line, at (0, 0, 0.14114) m, centred, pitched 1.5° wheels radius 0.05035 m, track ±0.103 m motor board 192.168.100.100:23 , UDP, 10-byte frames with CRC8-Maxim display 192.168.100.100:26 , UDP networks LiDAR 192.168.110.0/24 , motor/IO 192.168.100.0/24 Interfaces at a glance ¶ topic direction rate /scan from the LiDAR adapter ~14 Hz /odom , /motor_state/left , /motor_state/right from the motor driver 50 Hz /cmd_vel to the motor driver — the only actuation path — /cmd_vel/line , /cmd_vel/nav arbitration inputs to the mission — /line_then_home/state mission state on change /qrcode_text to the screen driver on change Services on the mission node: /line_then_home/start , …/stop , …/record_waypoints . Three things worth knowing up front ¶ The LiDAR sits at the centre of the body. A range reading is the distance to the centre; the body reaches 0.16 m further ahead. Obstacle checks account for this. Start the LiDAR first. Every ROS 2 process on this machine may compete for UDP 7000. bringup.launch.py orders it correctly. The motor driver has a watchdog. If commands stop, or motor feedback stops, the wheels are zeroed within half a second and the driver stays off until restarted.

docs.text: Running with caasi ¶ caasi deploys the project to a robot, builds it there, and runs each task as a tracked process you can watch, read and stop from your own machine. After the robot is enrolled (its SSH access set up and its host key recorded), everything below is driven from the project directory on your machine. No addresses or credentials are repeated per command. First time on a robot ¶ caasi deploy <target> # copy the project to the robot caasi build --target <target> # colcon build there, recorded against the deployment caasi deploy --status shows what is deployed and whether it verified. Run entry points ¶ Each task is one file in experiments/ . They all go through scripts/caasi_launch.py , which sources the ROS environment and then exec s the real command, so caasi run stop reaches ROS 2 the way Ctrl-C would. task experiment hardware bringup experiments/bringup.yaml bringup with teleoperation experiments/bringup_teleop.yaml bringup with rviz experiments/bringup_rviz.yaml mapping experiments/slam.yaml navigation experiments/navigation.yaml line-then-home mission experiments/mission.yaml mission with the site's line calibration experiments/mission_demo.yaml line follower alone experiments/line_follower.yaml obstacle guard alone experiments/obstacle_guard.yaml keyboard teleoperation alone experiments/teleop.yaml camera experiments/camera.yaml rviz experiments/rviz.yaml mission: start experiments/mission_start.yaml mission: stop experiments/mission_stop.yaml mission: record return waypoints experiments/mission_record_waypoints.yaml Running and watching ¶ caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t <target> caasi run status <run> caasi logs <run> -f caasi run stop <run> caasi run list The mission services are runs of their own, so a refused start shows up in the run status rather than scrolling past in a terminal: caasi run start experiments/mission_start.yaml -t <target> # prints success + message caasi run start experiments/mission_stop.yaml -t <target> Order that works for a mission ¶ caasi run start experiments/mission.yaml -t <target> # bringup + nav2 + mission + follower # set the pose (see Running on the robot) once nav2 is up # wait until all seven nav2 nodes report active caasi run start experiments/camera.yaml -t <target> # camera after nav2 caasi run start experiments/mission_start.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <mission run> -f # watch /line_then_home/state Bring nav2 up before the camera: the camera at full rate during bringup slows the lifecycle transitions considerably on a small machine. Where things land ¶ what where deployed project ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover on the robot run output <project>/.caasi/runs/<run>/stdout.log , stderr.log , exit_code run records ~/.caasi/runs/<run>/ on your machine Without caasi ¶ Every task above has a direct ROS 2 form; see Running on the robot and the full list in Commands and workflows . caasi is a convenience and a record keeper, not a requirement.

docs.text: Commands ¶ Every task, in the two places you might run it from: Local — on the robot itself. Both a plain ROS 2 command and a caasi run are given; they do the same thing, caasi adds a record. Remote — from another machine, through caasi. This is the normal way to operate a deployed robot. <target> is the execution target you enrolled in caasi. Each section also names the ROS 1 command it replaces, for comparison. 1. Bringup ¶ Starts the LiDAR adapter, both state publishers, the motor driver and the screen driver. Local # ROS 2 ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py # ROS 2 with rviz, or with the camera, or with a keyboard ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_visualization:=true ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_realsense:=true enable_teleop:=true # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t <target> caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f # follow the output caasi run status 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup caasi run stop 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup Check it worked ros2 topic hz /scan # ~14 Hz ros2 topic hz /odom # ~50 Hz ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once # fault flags false, rpm ~0 at rest ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch 2. Teleoperation ¶ Arrow keys drive and turn: 0.2 m/s and 0.4 rad/s, accelerating at 0.2 / 0.4 per second. Local # ROS 2 (a terminal on the robot's desktop) scripts/run_teleop.sh # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/teleop.yaml Remote Teleoperation needs the robot's display, so it is normally started as a run and driven while you watch the screen through a remote desktop session (see Remote access ): caasi run start experiments/teleop.yaml -t <target> caasi logs 20261022-101500-swjtumover-teleop -f Check it worked ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel # linear.x reaches ±0.2 while a key is held, 0 when released On a Wayland desktop the keyboard is only received while an X11 window has focus — click the rviz window first. Without any display the node exits with code 3 and says why. ROS 1: rosrun swjtumover_bringup teleop_node.py 3. Visualization ¶ Local # ROS 2 rviz2 -d "$(ros2 pkg prefix swjtumover_bringup)/share/swjtumover_bringup/config/bringup.rviz" # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/rviz.yaml Remote # start rviz with the bringup in one go caasi run start experiments/bringup_rviz.yaml -t <target> # or rviz against a bringup that is already running caasi run start experiments/rviz.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <the rviz run> -f Check it worked: the robot body, /scan and the camera image draw with only the bringup running. The /map panel fills once something publishes a map; the two costmap panels need nav2 and are off by default. ROS 1: rosrun rviz rviz -d $(rospack find swjtumover_bringup)/config/bringup.rviz 4. Mapping ¶ Local # ROS 2 ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup slam.launch.py # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/slam.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/slam.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <the slam run> -f Check it worked ros2 lifecycle get /slam_toolbox # active ros2 topic hz /map # ~0.3 Hz once the robot moves ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo map odom # the transform exists ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup bringup_gmapping.launch 5. Saving a map ¶ The target directory must exist; the service does not create it. Local mkdir -p ~/maps ros2 service call /slam_toolbox/save_map slam_toolbox/srv/SaveMap \ "{name: {data: '/home/swjtumover/maps/map'}}" Remote caasi exec --target <target> -- bash -c 'mkdir -p ~/maps && source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && \ ros2 service call /slam_toolbox/save_map slam_toolbox/srv/SaveMap \ "{name: {data: \"/home/swjtumover/maps/map\"}}"' | tail -2 nav2_map_server 's map_saver_cli does not work against slam_toolbox. ROS 1: rosrun map_server map_saver -f ~/maps/map 6. Navigation ¶ Local # ROS 2 -- serves the map, localises, plans and drives ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py # standalone test: let nav2 drive /cmd_vel directly ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py cmd_vel_topic:=/cmd_vel # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/navigation.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/navigation.yaml -t <target> Give it a pose — nav2 waits for one before activating its costmaps (the equivalent of rviz's "2D Pose Estimate"): ros2 topic pub --once /initialpose geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped \ "{header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {pose: {position: {x: 2.85, y: -2.77, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" Send a goal ros2 action send_goal /navigate_to_pose nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose \ "{pose: {header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {position: {x: 2.0, y: -2.0, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" \ --feedback Check it worked for n in map_server amcl planner_server controller_server behavior_server bt_navigator velocity_smoother; do printf '%-18s ' "$n"; ros2 lifecycle get "/$n" done Navigation publishes /cmd_vel/nav ; the mission node owns /cmd_vel . ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup map_server.launch , amcl.launch , move_base.launch 7. Line-then-home mission ¶ One launch brings up the bringup, all of nav2, the line follower and the mission — 21 nodes. Local ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup line_then_home.launch.py ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup line_then_home.launch.py map:=/path/to/nav.yaml follow_timeout:=60.0 Remote caasi run start experiments/mission.yaml -t <target> Start, stop and configure it — the services keep their ROS 1 names. # local ros2 service call /line_then_home/start std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" ros2 service call /line_then_home/record_waypoints std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" ros2 service call /line_then_home/stop std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" # remote caasi run start experiments/mission_start.yaml -t <target> caasi run start experiments/mission_record_waypoints.yaml -t <target> caasi run start experiments/mission_stop.yaml -t <target> The run prints what the service answered: /line_then_home/start: success=True message='task started: following the line' Check it worked ros2 topic echo /line_then_home/state # IDLE, FOLLOW, STOP, NAV, DONE, FAILED A successful run reads FOLLOW → STOP → NAV → DONE and ends where it started. The mission needs a pose first: it uses /amcl_pose when available and otherwise the map → base_link transform. The follower's image crop and colour range are launch arguments; experiments/mission_demo.yaml carries the values measured for the site's floor. ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup line_then_home.launch 8. Line follower on its own ¶ Local ros2 run swjtumover_bringup omove_following_feng.py --ros-args \ -p color_topic:=/camera/camera/color/image_raw \ -p depth_topic:=/camera/camera/depth/image_rect_raw # tuned for the site floor ros2 run swjtumover_bringup omove_following_feng.py --ros-args \ -p color_topic:=/camera/camera/color/image_raw \ -p depth_topic:=/camera/camera/depth/image_rect_raw \ -p roi_bottom_offset:=70 Remote caasi run start experiments/line_follower.yaml -t <target> Check it worked ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel # linear.x 0.12 with a steering term while the line is visible ros2 topic echo /reached_goal --once It stops when the line is lost, when the centre clearance falls below 0.28 m, and when it decides the line has ended; publishing true on /line_follow/enable clears that. ROS 1: python3 omove_following.py 9. Obstacle guard on its own ¶ Local ros2 run swjtumover_bringup obstacle_rplidar.py Remote caasi run start experiments/obstacle_guard.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <the guard run> -f # 'Go! path clear' then 'Stop! obstacle at ...' Drives forward at 0.2 m/s and stops when the ±10° front sector is closer than 0.85 m. ROS 1: python3 obstacle_rplidar.py 10. Camera ¶ Local ros2 launch realsense2_camera rs_launch.py ros2 topic hz /camera/camera/color/image_raw Remote caasi run start experiments/camera.yaml -t <target> Start it after nav2 is active and before starting the mission. ROS 1: roslaunch realsense2_camera rs_camera.launch (published /d415/... ) 11. Deploying and building ¶ Remote (caasi's purpose) caasi deploy <target> # copy the project to the robot caasi deploy <target> --status # what is deployed, and whether it verified caasi build --target <target> # colcon build there, recorded caasi build --target <target> --clean Local (on the robot) cd ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover colcon build --symlink-install source install/setup.bash Tests colcon test --packages-select swjtumover_bringup colcon test-result --result-base build/swjtumover_bringup 12. Inspection ¶ task ROS 2 example topic rate ros2 topic hz ros2 topic hz /scan one message ros2 topic echo --once ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once node list ros2 node list ros2 node list service call ros2 service call ros2 service call /line_then_home/stop std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" record a bag ros2 bag record ros2 bag record -o run1 /scan /odom /tf /motor_state/left transform tf2_echo ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo base_link lidar_link lifecycle state lifecycle get ros2 lifecycle get /amcl remote logs caasi logs caasi logs <run> -f remote processes caasi run list caasi run list remote occupancy caasi node occupancy caasi node occupancy

docs.text: Remote access and multiple robots ¶ Two practical questions once more than one robot runs this software: how to tell them apart, and how to see a robot's screen without sitting in front of it. Naming and identity ¶ Give caasi a target per machine , and let the software name stay swjtumover on all of them: targets: swjtumover-05: host: 10.212.19.94 user: swjtumover tags: [robot, swjtumover, jazzy] deployment_root: "~/caasi/robots/swjtumover" swjtumover-10: host: 10.212.19.104 user: swjtumover tags: [robot, swjtumover, jazzy] deployment_root: "~/caasi/robots/swjtumover" Why this shape: the tag says what it is — swjtumover identifies the robot family, so every machine running this software is found with one query regardless of its number; the target name says which machine — used for addressing, nothing else; deployment_root keeps the on-robot path constant — every robot deploys to ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover , so documentation, scripts and muscle memory are identical everywhere. caasi does not rely on the name to recognise a machine. Enrolment records the machine itself: machine_id = 2c7c442a1da846c6b70f5a2d7712d7db (/etc/machine-id, strong) cpu_model = Intel(R) N150 ssh keys: ecdsa / rsa / ed25519 with SHA256 fingerprints endpoint: 10.212.19.94:22, verified A renamed robot or a changed address is still the same robot, because acceptance requires a matching enrolled host key. A different machine answering on a reused address is refused. The same physical box can carry two targets when it dual-boots (one per operating system); they are distinguished by machine id, which is exactly what that field is for. Seeing the robot's screen remotely ¶ The robot runs GNOME on Wayland, so classic VNC servers do not apply — they can only capture X11 windows, not the desktop. GNOME's own remote desktop is already part of the system and streams only the regions that change, which keeps it usable on modest hardware. Enable it once, on the robot, as the desktop user: grdctl rdp set-credentials <user> <password> grdctl rdp disable-view-only # omit to stay read-only grdctl rdp enable grdctl status # expect Status: enabled, Port: 3389 Then reach it without exposing a port on the network, by tunnelling over the SSH access caasi already manages: ssh -N -L 3389:localhost:3389 <user>@<robot> and point a client at localhost:3389 : Remmina — remmina -c rdp://localhost:3389 FreeRDP — xfreerdp /v:localhost:3389 /u:<user> Install one of them on the machine you sit at ( apt install remmina or freerdp3-x11 ). grdctl status is also the health check: if it reports a missing or invalid certificate, re-running grdctl rdp enable regenerates one. Notes ¶ The display is only needed for interactive work. Bringup, mapping, navigation and the mission all run headless, and that is the normal mode on a robot. Interactive extras need the desktop session's display. scripts/run_teleop.sh resolves it automatically (the X cookie on a Wayland session is a file whose name changes per session). If a viewer must run on a weak machine, prefer this RDP path over browser-based viewers: the encoding cost stays on the machine that owns the screen.

docs.text: Hardware and safety ¶ Read this before driving the robot. Interfaces ¶ what where motor / IO board 192.168.100.100 , TCP/UDP 23 (motors) and UDP 26 (display) Vanjee 718H LiDAR 192.168.110.100 , UDP 7000 on the host and 5000 on the LiDAR host addresses 192.168.100.10 (motor network), 192.168.110.10 (LiDAR network) The motor protocol is the board's own: 10-byte datagrams, CRC8-Maxim in the last byte, motor id 0x01 left / 0x02 right, speed as a signed RPM. Only the motor driver should talk to port 23. Safety model ¶ layer behaviour command watchdog motor.cmd_vel_timeout (0.5 s): no new /cmd_vel means zero speed feedback watchdog motor.motor_feedback_timeout (0.5 s): lost telemetry means zero speed, and the driver stays off until restarted fault latch any board fault flag (over-temperature, stall, phase overcurrent, overcurrent, sensor) latches the driver off body-aware guard the line follower holds zero when the centre clearance falls below 0.28 m navigation nav2's footprint critic rejects trajectories that would put the body into an obstacle A latched driver stays off deliberately: it means something real happened. Restart it after fixing the cause. Geometry ¶ The body is 0.32 × 0.30 m and the LiDAR is at its centre, so every range reading is measured to the centre while the body extends 0.16 m further forward. The line follower stops at 0.28 m of centre clearance (0.16 m body plus 0.12 m margin); nav2 uses the body footprint with footprint_padding: 0.06 . A single-line LiDAR sweeps one plane at 0.141 m. Objects shorter than that plane are not seen. Before driving ¶ Check the supply. The motor board goes quiet when the battery sags — it still answers ping while the protocol replies decay. If replies fall below roughly 95 %, charge it. Start the LiDAR first. Whichever process binds UDP 7000 keeps it; if the motor driver wins, there is no /scan . Never leave a publisher running. Every script here publishes a final zero and the watchdog covers the rest, but do not walk away from a live publisher. Set a pose before navigating. nav2 activates its global costmap only once map → base_link exists. Health checks ¶ ping -c3 192.168.100.100 # board reachable ros2 topic hz /scan # ~14 Hz ros2 topic hz /odom # ~50 Hz ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once # fault flags false, rpm ~0 at rest ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo base_link lidar_link # z = 0.14114 m, roll = 1.500° If something does not work ¶ symptom cause action no /scan another process holds UDP 7000 restart with the bringup, which orders it correctly no /odom , driver logs a feedback timeout then latches board silent: supply, cabling charge or repair, then restart the driver nav2 nodes stay inactive no map → base_link publish /initialpose map_server fails to configure map yaml path wrong image: in the yaml must be relative the robot does not move although /cmd_vel carries values driver latched, or the controller is publishing to /cmd_vel/nav restart the driver; check cmd_vel_topic keyboard teleoperation does nothing no X11 focus on a Wayland desktop click the rviz window, then use the arrow keys

docs.text: Running on the robot ¶ Everything here runs on the robot itself, with ROS 2 Jazzy. Build ¶ colcon build --symlink-install source install/setup.bash Run the tests: colcon test --packages-select swjtumover_bringup colcon test-result --result-base build/swjtumover_bringup Hardware bringup ¶ ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py Starts the LiDAR adapter first, then robot_state_publisher , joint_state_publisher , motor_node and screen_node . ros2 topic hz /scan # ~14 Hz ros2 topic hz /odom # ~50 Hz ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once # fault flags false at rest Optional parts are launch arguments, all off by default because the robot is normally headless: ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_visualization:=true # rviz ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_teleop:=true # keyboard ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_realsense:=true # camera Teleoperation ¶ scripts/run_teleop.sh Arrow keys drive and turn: 0.2 m/s and 0.4 rad/s, accelerating at 0.2 / 0.4 per second. The script resolves the display and X cookie itself and loads config/teleop.yaml . If the keys do nothing, give an X11 window focus first — on a Wayland desktop pynput only receives keys while an Xwayland window is focused. Mapping ¶ ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup slam.launch.py Check it with ros2 lifecycle get /slam_toolbox (expect active ) and ros2 topic hz /map (about 0.3 Hz once the robot moves). Save the map with slam_toolbox's service; the directory must already exist: mkdir -p ~/maps ros2 service call /slam_toolbox/save_map slam_toolbox/srv/SaveMap \ "{name: {data: '/home/swjtumover/maps/map'}}" nav2_map_server 's map_saver_cli does not work against slam_toolbox; use the service above. Navigation ¶ ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py nav2 comes up waiting for a pose. Give it one, the equivalent of rviz's "2D Pose Estimate": ros2 topic pub --once /initialpose geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped \ "{header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {pose: {position: {x: 2.85, y: -2.77, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" All seven nav2 nodes then become active : map_server , amcl , planner_server , controller_server , behavior_server , bt_navigator , velocity_smoother . Send a goal with rviz, or: ros2 action send_goal /navigate_to_pose nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose \ "{pose: {header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {position: {x: 2.0, y: -2.0, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" Two things to know: nav2 publishes /cmd_vel/nav , not /cmd_vel . The mission node owns /cmd_vel and arbitrates between the line follower and navigation. For a standalone navigation test, add cmd_vel_topic:=/cmd_vel . the default map is map/nav_maze.yaml , the maze region of the site map with world coordinates preserved. map:=<path>/nav.yaml uses the whole building, which is slower as a nav2 costmap. Useful launch arguments: set_initial_pose:=true initial_pose_x:=… initial_pose_y:=… initial_pose_yaw:=… . The line-then-home mission ¶ ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup line_then_home.launch.py ros2 service call /line_then_home/start std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" ros2 service call /line_then_home/stop std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" ros2 service call /line_then_home/record_waypoints std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" ros2 topic echo /line_then_home/state # IDLE, FOLLOW, STOP, NAV, DONE, FAILED That one launch brings up the hardware bringup, all of nav2, the line follower and the mission together — 21 nodes. argument default purpose map map/nav_maze.yaml map to serve color_topic , depth_topic /camera/camera/... images for the line follower start_hardware true set false if the bringup already runs lidar_bind_lead 3.0 passed to the bringup so the LiDAR wins UDP 7000 follower_roi_top_offset , follower_roi_bottom_offset 100 , 0 the follower's image crop follower_line_lower , follower_line_upper [10,20,10] , [40,50,40] its colour range follower_end_confirm_frames 5 frames before the end of the line counts follow_timeout 300.0 seconds of following before moving on The follower starts disabled and is enabled by /line_then_home/start , so the mission remains the only publisher of /cmd_vel . Start the robot on the line with a valid pose; the mission records where it started and returns there. Individual behaviours ¶ ros2 run swjtumover_bringup obstacle_rplidar.py # forward, stop inside 0.85 m ros2 run swjtumover_bringup omove_following_feng.py # follow the black line ros2 run swjtumover_bringup teleop_node.py # keyboard The line follower needs colour and depth images; with realsense2_camera : ros2 run swjtumover_bringup omove_following_feng.py --ros-args \ -p color_topic:=/camera/camera/color/image_raw \ -p depth_topic:=/camera/camera/depth/image_rect_raw It drives at 0.12 m/s and steers in proportion to the line's offset. It stops when the line is lost, when the front sector closes to 0.28 m, and when it decides the line has ended — publishing true on /line_follow/enable clears that. Visualization ¶ rviz2 -d "$(ros2 pkg prefix swjtumover_bringup)/share/swjtumover_bringup/config/bringup.rviz" The robot model, /scan and the camera image draw as soon as the bringup is running. The map panel fills once something publishes /map . The two costmap panels are off by default because they need nav2. Camera ¶ ros2 launch realsense2_camera rs_launch.py It publishes under /camera/camera/... . Start it after nav2 has reached active .
